title: Clinton Crushes Sanders in South Carolina – Now She's Coming for Trump!
text: Fresh off a crushing landslide in Saturday's South Carolina primary, Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton has turned her guns on Donald Trump, the favorite for the Republican nomination, and a possible showdown in the Nov. 8 presidential election. She didn't even need to say his name. "Despite what you hear, we don't need to make America great again. America has never stopped being great," she told cheering supporters in her South Carolina victory speech, a pointed jab at his campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again." Clinton insisted she was taking nothing for granted after flattening Democratic rival Bernie Sanders on Saturday by a staggering 48 percentage points, likely setting herself up for a big "Super Tuesday" night on March 1, a key date in the nomination battle. And if Clinton and Trump both win big on Tuesday, as opinion polls suggest? Then a Clinton-Trump general election clash becomes ever more likely, yet another twist in a presidential campaign that has defied convention as U.S. voters vent their frustration over economic uncertainty, illegal immigration and national security threats. Some Clinton backers, fired up by the growing chance of a Trump nomination, have doubled down on their support for the former secretary of state, insisting that she, not Sanders, is the one best equipped to take down Trump in a head-to-head showdown in November. Rosilyne Scott, 58, of Texas, cast her vote early for Clinton ahead of Texas's Tuesday nominating contest, calling the prospect of a Trump presidency "frightening." "I just think she has more support, and she's been doing it a lot longer," she said. "If you get someone like Donald Trump in, I don't know. ... I think he's a joke, a bigot, a racist." And with Clinton's momentum surging against Sanders, a U.S. senator from Vermont, donors have found fresh resolve too.

title: Report: Hillary Clinton to raise $1 billion to unseat Republican representatives and senators
text: As the primary season advances and states hold their contests, the Clinton campaign is moving quickly to extend its advantage over the Republicans. According to a report by Politico, Hillary Clinton and her campaign plan to raise more than $1 billion to unseat vulnerable House and Senate Republicans, with the aim of taking 10 to 25 House seats from Republicans and regaining control of the Senate. The report stated: "Hillary Clinton will raise $1 billion for Democrats and the party will train some of their efforts and that money on defeating House and Senate Republicans. Party leaders privately concede that the Senate could be lost either way. But senior House Republicans say they're in good shape across the country, and see no evidence that the control of the chamber is in play." Republicans are particularly concerned by these reports, given that the Republican National Committee fell almost $10 million short of its July fundraising predictions, raising only $27 million. In the same month, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the fundraising arm of the Democratic National Committee, raised more than $35 million, not including a total of $90 million in joint fundraising with Clinton, and has raised almost $20 million more than the RNC so far in the 2016 fiscal year. Trump, by contrast, had a very good month for fundraising. Compared with the RNC's weak monthly figures, the numbers indicate that the GOP is placing its trust and its money in Trump alone. While Trump is harming down-ballot candidates and their re-election efforts, Clinton is set to raise unprecedented amounts of money for the Democrats while also funding her own campaign. In May 2015, Politico reported that Clinton's campaign aimed to raise more than $2 billion by the time of the November general election.

title: Another Russian dies: Stanislav Petrov, who prevented nuclear war, found dead
text: It has emerged that Stanislav Petrov, a former Soviet Lieutenant Colonel, died on May 19 this year in his apartment in the small town of Fryazino, northeast of Moscow. Petrov is not widely known, but without his actions, or lack of action, there is a good chance that many people alive today would not be here. The 2014 film The Man Who Saved The World, starring Kevin Costner, was based on how Petrov prevented a nuclear crisis between the US and the USSR, and averted the potential for World War III, in the 1980s by essentially doing nothing at all. This may be part of the reason Petrov never considered himself a hero. "At first when people started telling me that these TV reports had started calling me a hero, I was surprised. I never thought of myself as one after all, I was literally just doing my job," he said in an interview later in life. On September 26, 1983, Petrov was on duty in a bunker near Moscow, in charge of an early warning radar system. Shortly after midnight, Petrov noticed a single missile on the screen, launched from the US and heading toward the Soviet Union. "When I first saw the alert message, I got up from my chair. All my subordinates were confused, so I started shouting orders at them to avoid panic. I knew my decision would have a lot of consequences," Petrov recalled in a 2010 interview. "The siren went off for a second time. Giant blood-red letters appeared on our main screen, saying START."

title: Travel Ban Fallout: Tourism Chief Warns America Will Keep Bleeding Visitors!
text: Tweaking it changes nothing! That is the blunt warning from the head of the UN World Tourism Organization: U.S. President Donald Trump's revised travel ban on citizens of certain Muslim-majority countries will hit tourism just as hard. "People don't go to places where they don't feel welcome," said Taleb Rifai, the tourism organization's secretary general, ahead of the opening on Wednesday of the world's biggest travel trade fair, ITB Berlin. On Monday Trump signed a revised executive order banning citizens of six Muslim-majority nations from traveling to the United States, dropping Iraq from the list after his controversial first attempt was blocked by the courts. But Rifai was not impressed. "It's not about the details of which countries are included, it's about the attitude," he said on Tuesday. And the cost? Last week he said the United States had lost a whopping $185 million in a single month after the first ban was introduced, and stood to lose tens of millions more every month if similar policies continued. Data from travel analysis company ForwardKeys this week showed that demand for travel to the United States in the coming months had already flattened out after a positive start to the year. Yet the rest of the world will barely notice: any slump in demand for travel to the United States is not expected to affect travel in general. International tourist numbers are expected to grow 3 to 4 percent this year from last year's 1.24 billion, Rifai said on Tuesday. "The world has opened up in incredible ways. There are so many options now. If you want to gamble, you don't have to go to Las Vegas, you can go to Macau instead," he said. Ouch! Market researcher Euromonitor has slashed its forecast for U.S. arrivals by 2020 to 84.2 million from 85.2 million amid the uncertainty over the travel ban.

title: Tillerson Pushes Senate to Let Montenegro Into NATO – Defying Moscow!
text: Russia won't like this. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson has written to the leaders of the U.S. Senate urging them to ratify Montenegro as NATO's newest member, calling it "strongly in the interests of the United States." In a letter dated March 7 and seen on Tuesday, Tillerson argued that Montenegro joining the alliance would support greater integration, democratic reform, trade, security and stability among its neighbors. Moscow fiercely opposes any further expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. And the delay in U.S. approval of Montenegro's accession has raised pointed questions: will President Donald Trump's administration and his Republican Party stand up to Russia, despite Trump's desire for better relations? The letter surfaced in the middle of a row over the new secretary of state's relationship with the alliance. It was reported on Monday that Tillerson planned to skip a meeting with NATO foreign ministers next month so he could stay home for a visit by China's president, while planning a trip to Russia later in April. Then, on Tuesday, a U-turn: the administration proposed new dates for the meeting, which had been set for April 5 and 6 in Brussels. Montenegro, a tiny former Yugoslav republic with a population of 650,000, hopes to win the required approval of all 28 NATO allies in time to become a full member at a summit in May. By early this month, 24 had approved. NATO members see Montenegro's accession as a way to push back against Russia's efforts to expand its influence in the Balkans. But at least two Republican senators, Rand Paul and Mike Lee, have blocked a quick vote in the full U.S. Senate for months, and Senate leaders have not scheduled a more time-consuming roll-call vote.

title: Scalia's death throws the biggest abortion case in years wide open!
text: The timing could not be more dramatic. The sudden death of Justice Antonin Scalia comes less than a month before the Supreme Court hears its biggest abortion case in a decade. The best outcome for abortion rights opponents? A 4-4 tie. In that case, Supreme Court rules say the circuit court's decision stays in place without setting any constitutional precedent.

title: Abe's landslide: Japan's leader puts schools before budget – and markets soar!
text: A thumping win, and a bold pledge. Japan's prime minister has vowed to put education and childcare ahead of balancing the budget after winning a fresh mandate from voters on Sunday, as a rapidly ageing population threatens to wreck his efforts to reflate the economy. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's ruling coalition stormed to a landslide victory at the polls, powered by his campaign promises to pour more money into education and childcare, partly to get more women into the workforce. Abe also made it clear he would keep pushing cautious Japanese firms to spend their record cash piles on raising employees' wages to fire up a virtuous growth cycle. With his Abenomics recipe of hyper-easy monetary policy set to continue, Abe's solid win also boosted expectations that he would reappoint Bank of Japan Governor Haruhiko Kuroda in early April when his five-year term ends. The markets cheered! Abe's victory lifted world stocks and the dollar on Monday, sending Japan's Nikkei share average to 21-year highs. The index closed up 1.1 percent at 21,696.65, its record 15th straight gain. Abe swept to power in late 2012, promising to drag Japan's economy, the world's third largest, out of nearly two decades of deflation and stagnation. Has he done it? The economy is recovering slowly, but sluggish wage growth is holding back consumer spending and inflation, while companies struggle with labor shortages caused by a low birth rate and fast-ageing population. The premier promised free pre-school for all children aged three to five and for children aged two or below from low-income households. "The key to Japan's sustainable growth is how we respond to ageing of the population, which is the biggest challenge for Abenomics," Abe told a news conference.

title: Turkey erupts over EU headscarf ruling: 'Quo vadis Europa?'
text: Turkey is furious. On Tuesday it lashed out at a ruling by the EU's top court that European companies can ban employees from wearing religious or political symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, saying it would fuel 'anti-Muslim trends'. "The European Court of Justice decision on the headscarf today will only strengthen and xenophobic trends," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's spokesman Ibrahim Kalin said in a tweet. Then the jab: "Quo vadis Europa? (Where is Europe going? )" he added. The broadside came as Turkey is locked in a bitter row with Germany, the Netherlands and other EU states over the blocking of Turkish officials from holding rallies abroad in the campaign for a referendum on expanding Erdogan's powers. What did the court actually say? The European Court of Justice (ECJ) said it does not constitute "direct discrimination" if a firm has an internal rule banning the wearing of "any political, philosophical or religious sign." The court was weighing the case of a Muslim woman fired by the security company G4S in Belgium after she insisted on wearing a headscarf. And the irony! Just last month Turkey said it was lifting a historic ban on female officers wearing the Islamic headscarf in the country's officially secular armed forces, the last institution where the garment was forbidden.

title: Pentagon suspends recovery of National Guard signing bonuses
text: Defense Secretary Ashton B. Carter announced on Wednesday that the Pentagon is suspending its program to recover military signing bonuses. The announcement is a welcome development in a situation that should never have arisen. Nearly 10,000 California National Guard veterans had been pursued to repay money that was mistakenly given to them for re-enlisting at the height of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. The demands for repayment were not only ungrateful but also poor strategy. A recent high school or college graduate considering career options may be approached by a recruiter who promises a generous bonus. In exchange, the recruit agrees to spend a few years being told where to live, where to work and what time to wake up, while also facing the possibility of being shot or blown up and killed. The recruit would also be required to submit to a justice system that could send a service member to prison for a disagreement with a superior. The article was written by Charles E. Schmidt. It was posted by Arnaldo Rodgers, a trained and educated psychologist who has worked as a community organizer and activist.

title: Catalonia gridlocked: strikers choke roads in fury over jailed leaders!
text: Chaos on the roads. A strike called across Catalonia by pro-independence activists, furious at the jailing of sacked regional politicians, brought roads to a standstill early on Wednesday, causing huge tailbacks into Barcelona while some public transport ran only minimum services. The Catalan pro-independence union CSC called the strike, backed by civic groups Asamblea Nacional Catalana (ANC) and Omnium Cultural, whose leaders were thrown in prison last month on sedition charges. Scores of people blocked dozens of major highways in the region, waving placards and chanting "freedom for political prisoners", while minor scuffles were reported on social media as police tried to move protesters, TV and video images showed. In the city of Girona, one crowd of activists even forced their way into the train station and protested on the tracks, causing delays, images on social media showed. And yet? Despite the transport delays, shops and businesses in the region largely seemed to be working as normal. The leaders of the ANC and Omnium and eight former members of the Catalan government are in prison awaiting trial after staging a referendum on secession that Spanish courts deemed illegal and then declaring independence. The independence drive has plunged Spain into its worst political crisis in decades, deepening political and cultural divisions and driving thousands of companies to relocate out of the region. The government, which seized control of Catalonia after a unilateral independence declaration, has called an election for Dec. 21. Will it end the crisis?

title: Amber Heard donates $350,000 to the ACLU
text: Actress Amber Heard is donating $350,000 to the ACLU as the civil rights organization prepares to oppose the incoming Donald Trump administration. The money comes from Heard's settlement in her divorce from actor Johnny Depp, in which domestic violence allegations were made. TMZ reported that it had received an email from the ACLU in which an ACLU representative acknowledged that Amber made a $350k payment on August 19th. According to a source connected with Amber who spoke to TMZ, she advanced the money, relying on Johnny paying her the settlement. TMZ also reported that she took steps to send money to Children's Hospital but did not send it because she and Johnny began disputing the settlement deal. Amber's lawyer, Pierce O'Donnell, says he is confident the settlement will be signed this week. During the campaign, the ACLU described Trump as a one-man Constitutional crisis and warned that his statements and policy proposals would blatantly violate the inalienable rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The ACLU was one of the first organizations to issue a strong statement against Trump after he won the 2016 election: "President-elect Trump, as you assume the nation's highest office, we urge you to reconsider and change course on certain campaign promises you have made. These include your plan to amass a deportation force to remove 11 million undocumented immigrants; ban the entry of Muslims into our country and aggressively surveil them; punish women for accessing abortion; reauthorize waterboarding and other forms of torture; and change our nation's libel laws and restrict freedom of expression. These proposals are not simply un-American and wrong-headed, they are unlawful and unconstitutional. They violate the First, Fourth, Fifth, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments."
